content:
Cover photo blurred to protect my location.
Intro I don’t love handing over my sensitive data to Big Tech. When I considered getting a home surveillance system to watch my cat, I worried about where that data was ending up.
So I thought why not keep it local.
After a bit of research I found Frigate NVR which addressed all my concerns and came with some pretty powerful features to play with.
Below I talk about how I configured Frigate with object detection, face recognition, and more on afforadable hardware!
Hardware Cameras Prices below as of 2026:
- 4x Tapo C101 (Used on Amazon - $50) - 2x Tapo C217 (Amazon - $60) Im using the C101 camera model indoors and the C217 outdoors.
Both of these models support RTSP; the C217 also supports pan/tilt features over ONVIF. PC Hardware You will want a mid-range PC with a decent GPU or a Raspberry Pi to run Frigate.
Object detection will be best with an AI Coprocessor. If you dont have one but want to test out detection, you could also configure a dedicated GPU to run a lightweight model.
I’m using the Google Coral TPU USB Accelerator (Amazon - ~$100) to run my object detection. This is only one option of many. See Frigate docs for more.
My GPU is an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 purchased nearly 10 years ago. All I need it for is rendering the camera stream, but it handles lightweight AI models just fine through the ONNX format.
Total cost for cameras and AI Coprocessor: $210.00
Software PC Environment Docker Frigate runs on Docker. Some experience here will go a long way, but it’s doable for a beginner and Frigate thorough [documentation(https://docs.frigate.video/frigate/installation/#docker).
Make sure you’re comfortable with creating containers with a docker-compose.yaml config file, bind mounting, port mapping, and reading the build time logs. These skills will be helpful if things go south.
Operating System My flavor of Linux is CachyOS. I find Linux a bit more compatible with Docker, but I’ve also spun up Frigate containers in Windows no problem. Tailscale Spinning up a container on your home PC is great for keeping your data local, but it’s not very useful if you can’t deploy outside your home network.
That’s where Tailscale comes in!
The use for Tailscale in this context is to set up a private network (Tailnet) where we can control who gets in through a convenient desktop or mobile app. That way I can route my home network traffic through a Zero Trust connectivity platform to devices pretty much anywhere.
I won’t bother going over set up of Tailscale; it’s quite painless. Just make sure you read up on security and understand the risk.
Cameras The Tapo cameras require you to create an account for setup. Upon initial setup, the cameras are configured to stream directly to TP-Links proprietary cloud platform. This is something I wanted to avoid in favor of using RTSP to receive streams locally and preventing the cameras from directly accessing the internet.
NOTE: TP-Link does not make it easy to keep the camera streams isolated from external servers.
You must first create a TP-Link account to boot the cameras, create an RTSP stream account for each camera, then configure a static IP for each camera.
In order to prevent camera streams from reaching Tapo servers, you must configure each camera with a bad gateway after setting up the streams in Frigate.
This will immediately kick the cameras offline according to the Tapo app, but you can keep tapping into the RTSP streams.
Now you have camera streams over WiFi, and the data never leaves your network!
Object Detection Note: In order to use object detection you must also configure motion detection.
The quality of your object detections is going to be dependent on a few key parameters:
- Model Choice - Input Resolution - Variant Size (if using YOLOv9 models) I’m using the small variant of YOLOv9 with an input resolution of 320x320. You might think running larger input resolution would produce better results, but this is not the case.
320x320 actually has a better shot at detecting small objects than a 640x640 input; the model is only able to fit more objects into a single detection if the resolution is increased.
Once you’ve configured motion detection and object detection, Frigate will start handing over detections to review.
The categories of object Frigate will show you depend on what your model choice is capable of, the labels file you hand over to your model, and what you have configured Frigate to show you.
Semantic Search One of the coolest features available on Frigate is Semantic Search.
This feature takes object detections and runs them through another Local AI model (from Jina AI) which gives the images embeddings. These embeddings provide text descriptions of the image to group relevant images together.
From there, you can search through your database of detections based on the embeddings…
For example, here I search my detection database for the term “white shirt”:
Just think of the possibilities!
Face Recognition Setting up facial recognition is very intuitive. Simply add some clear images of the subjects face and Frigate will start classifying people detected with sub_labels based on their face.
You can also train these facial detections easily and directly in the user interface. It is crucial you train based on a set of high quality images with diverse lighting, orientation, etc.
Training on a poor dataset will quickly degrade the quality of your classifications.
You also want to avoid training on images that were already classified with a relatively high score. This could lead to overfitting.
Outro So that’s a brief write-up on how I’m using Frigate. There are still plenty of features I want to try out (object states, zones, license plate recognition, and more).
If I get the sense enough people care I may end up creating a full tutorial and sharing my anonymized configuration file and Docker Compose file.
’til next time!
